title: Ezekiel 47:1–12
context: The prophet reports that the man who has guided him through the temple vision (40:3) brings him back to the door of the house, where water flows out from under the threshold toward the east, and measures the stream as it deepens from ankle-deep to a river too deep to cross, asking him, “Son of man, have you seen this?” The man then explains that the waters go down into the Arabah and toward the sea, so that the waters are healed, fish abound, and trees on both banks bear fruit every month, “and its leaf for healing,” while the swamps and marshes are left to salt. The river is a picture of hope, life flowing from God’s presence, and readers in both traditions name related images in Zechariah 14:8, John 7:38, and Revelation 22:1–2 without merging them, while place identifications such as the Arabah, the sea, En Gedi, and En Eglaim are held with varying confidence.

verses.text: He brought me back to the door of the temple; and behold, waters flowed out from under the threshold of the temple eastward, for the front of the temple faced toward the east. The waters came down from underneath, from the right side of the temple, on the south of the altar.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet says, “waters flowed out from under the threshold of the temple eastward.” Arminian readers note that the water’s source is the house where the LORD’s glory has returned (43:4–5).

Life flows from God’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the river as a gift that begins with God and not with human effort.

Shared ground: both traditions read the river as an image of blessing flowing from the place where God dwells (cf. Ps 46:4; Joel 3:18), whatever view they take of chapters 40–48 as a whole.

verses.text: Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me around by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east. Behold, waters ran out on the right side.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man leads the prophet “by the way of the gate northward” and around to the outer east gate, where “waters ran out on the right side.” Arminian readers note that the stream continues beyond the temple’s walls.

The east gate is the way the glory returned (43:4).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the blessing moving outward from the sanctuary.

Shared ground: both traditions note the careful route of the guide and read it as part of the vision’s movement from the house of God to the land.

verses.text: When the man went out eastward with the line in his hand, he measured one thousand cubits, and he caused me to pass through the waters, waters that were to the ankles.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When the man went out eastward with the line in his hand, he measured one thousand cubits.” Arminian readers note that the measuring line, used for the temple, now measures the river.

The waters are “to the ankles.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the river measured with the same care given to the house.

Shared ground: both traditions read the measured stages as showing that the water grows as it flows, a picture of increasing blessing rather than a map of depths.

verses.text: Again he measured one thousand, and caused me to pass through the waters, waters that were to the knees. Again he measured one thousand, and caused me to pass through waters that were to the waist.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man measures another thousand, then another, and the waters reach “to the knees” and then “to the waist.” Arminian readers note the steady deepening of the stream.

No tributaries are mentioned; the growth comes from the source.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the increase as the work of God’s provision.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the image points to abundance growing from God’s presence, while holding precise symbolism for each stage lightly.

verses.text: Afterward he measured one thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass through, for the waters had risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be walked through.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet says, “it was a river that I could not pass through, for the waters had risen, waters to swim in.” Arminian readers note that the stream has become more than he can cross.

The blessing outgrows human measure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the river exceeding what human strength can manage.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope: what begins as a trickle becomes a river that cannot be walked through, a picture of God’s overflowing grace.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, have you seen this?” Then he brought me and caused me to return to the bank of the river.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man asks, “Son of man, have you seen this?” and then brings the prophet back to the bank. Arminian readers note that “son of man” is the prophet’s usual title in the book.

The question invites careful attention.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the title as the LORD’s way of addressing his human messenger, with no point of disagreement attached.

Shared ground: both traditions hear the guide’s question as a summons to take in what the river means before it is explained.

verses.text: Now when I had returned, behold, on the bank of the river were very many trees on the one side and on the other.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet says that “on the bank of the river were very many trees on the one side and on the other.” Arminian readers note the sudden picture of abundant growth.

The trees will be explained in 47:12.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see life springing up where the river flows.

Shared ground: both traditions note the echo of garden imagery (cf. Gen 2:9–10) and of Revelation 22:2, named here without merging the passages.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “These waters flow out toward the eastern region and will go down into the Arabah. Then they will go toward the sea and flow into the sea which will be made to flow out; and the waters will be healed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man says, “These waters flow out toward the eastern region and will go down into the Arabah,” and into the sea, “and the waters will be healed.” Arminian readers note the promise of healing.

The sea is commonly taken to be the Dead Sea, though the text does not name it here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a picture of renewal reaching even barren places.

Shared ground: both traditions hold the geographical identifications with care and agree that the main point is life and healing where there was none.

verses.text: It will happen that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man says that “everything will live wherever the river comes.” Arminian readers note the abundance of living creatures and fish.

The river reverses death and barrenness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the life-giving power of what flows from God’s sanctuary.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope, and many in both traditions connect it with the life Christ gives (cf. John 7:38), while letting Ezekiel’s picture stand on its own.

verses.text: It will happen that fishermen will stand by it. From En Gedi even to En Eglaim will be a place for the spreading of nets. Their fish will be after their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceedingly many.
verses.arminianNotes:
The man says “fishermen will stand by it,” and “From En Gedi even to En Eglaim will be a place for the spreading of nets.” Arminian readers note that ordinary work flourishes in the renewed land.

En Gedi is usually placed by the Dead Sea; En Eglaim is less certain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the blessing reaching daily life and labor.

Shared ground: both traditions hold the place identifications lightly and agree that the image is of plenty, with fish “exceedingly many.”

verses.text: But its swamps and marshes will not be healed. They will be given up to salt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But its swamps and marshes will not be healed. They will be given up to salt.” Arminian readers note that not every place is transformed.

The reason is not given, and readers suggest several possibilities, including a continued source of salt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the meaning of this detail lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions avoid building doctrine on the verse and read it as part of the vision’s realistic texture, without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: By the river banks, on both sides, will grow every tree for food, whose leaf won’t wither, neither will its fruit fail. It will produce new fruit every month, because its waters issue out of the sanctuary. Its fruit will be for food, and its leaf for healing.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The trees bear fruit every month, “because its waters issue out of the sanctuary. Its fruit will be for food, and its leaf for healing.” Arminian readers note that food and healing come from God’s presence.

Revelation 22:2 uses similar language.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the source of all the river’s blessing in the sanctuary.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of provision and healing, naming Revelation 22:1–2 in passing without harmonizing the details.
